title: ‘Chicago PD’s’ Jesse Lee Soffer, Matt Olmstead to Develop ‘Strike Force’ Drama at CBS, Jerry Bruckheimer to Produce
description:
CBS is developing a new law enforcement drama that hails from two “One Chicago” mainstays. 

	Variety has learned that CBS has opened a development
body:
CBS is developing a new law enforcement drama that hails from two “One Chicago” mainstays. 

	Variety has learned that CBS has opened a development room for the series, titled “Strike Force.” Matt Olmstead is writing and executive producing the new series, while Jesse Lee Soffer will star and executive produce. Jerry Bruckheimer and KristieAnne Reed also executive produce via Jerry Bruckheimer TV. CBS Studios will produce. 


	The logline for the show states, “A battle-tested DEA agent (Soffer) returns home to Kansas City to lead a multi-agency strike force targeting the violent criminals now trying to exploit America’s heartland.” 
	

	The show is being developed to potentially launch during the 2027-2028 broadcast season. 

	Soffer is best known for his role as Senior Detective Jay Halstead in “Chicago PD,” which Olmstead co-created with Dick Wolf and on which he served as showrunner for four seasons. Soffer starred in the show for 10 seasons before departing. He and Olmstead then re-teamed on fellow Wolf Entertainment show “FBI: International” at CBS, with Soffer joining the show for its fourth and final season. Olmstead was a writer and executive producer on that series. 

	Soffer also appeared in both “Chicago Med” and “Chicago Fire” during his time with “Chicago PD,” as well as in a crossover with “Law & Order: SVU.” His other TV roles include “As the World Turns.” 

	He is repped by UTA and Ethos Entertainment. 

	More to come…

schema.headline: ‘Chicago PD’s’ Jesse Lee Soffer, Matt Olmstead to Develop ‘Strike Force’ Drama at CBS, Jerry Bruckheimer to Produce

title: Jon Favreau on His First Documentary, National Geographic’s ‘Lion’: Not Knowing Whether the Lead Character Would Survive Was ‘Harrowing’
description: When renowned wildlife producer Mike Gunton approached “The Lion King” director Jon Favreau about collaborating on a documentary, the director, who
body:
When renowned wildlife producer Mike Gunton approached “The Lion King” director Jon Favreau about collaborating on a documentary, the director, who had never made a doc, immediately said yes.
	It was 2022, and Gunton, an executive producer at BBC Studios Natural History Unit, wanted to “supersize” his “Dynasties” series about vulnerable or endangered species, and make a multipart doc focused on one species. At the time Favreau and Gunton were working together on the first season of “Prehistoric Planet,” a natural-history show that tells the last days of the dinosaur using CGI.
	
	“It wasn’t like I wanted to do a documentary,” said Favreau. “It was more that I really enjoyed working with Mike and his team. They went from my world — the digital world and then I went to their world, which was the documentary.”

	Over the course of four years, Favreau and Gunton worked with a production team that included producers, researchers, editors and cinematographers Simon Blakeney and Sophie Darlington to create National Geographic’s “Lion.”
	“Mike had the ambition of following a single pride of lions in a way that had never been done before, and it meant hanging up all the tools that I was comfortable with, like CGI, and going completely analog,” said Favreau. “We made a rule that we were not going to do any digital augmentation, not paint things out, and not manipulate the footage.” 
	The four-part series follows a lion cub named Kio, who faces loss, exile and fierce rivals in a fight to survive and become a king. Filmed in Kenya’s Maasai Mara, “Lion” is the first natural history production to document a lion’s complete journey from cub to king. The crew, including local Kenyan filmmaker Faith Musembi, logged nearly 1,400 filming days across 52 shoots — the most time ever spent in the field exclusively following a single pride. It was a daunting project that Gunton knew Favreau would be interested in executive producing, and not just because he had directed both the 2019 live-action remake of the animated classic “The Lion King” and “The Jungle Book.”“When we first met, Jon told me that he had been using “Dynasties” as a reference for how (lions) moved, how they behaved, and what their little micro movements were while making “The Lion King,” said Gunton. “So, there was an immediate simpatico between us because he was fascinated by the logistics, the grammar, the style, the approach, and all the storytelling techniques in a documentary like ‘Dynasties.’”
	
	To find a main character for “Lion,” the crew initially followed two prides in the Maasai Mara. Family trees were drawn up. Each lion in both prides had its own identification card, where details down to the whisker spots were logged. The production team relied on a network of local field guides to help them track the lions, who could be hard to find when hidden in bushes or mile after mile of long grass. Eventually the crew could identify up to 50 lions from different prides by name and family relationships. “We were following prides, and within them there were male cubs, female cubs, big, powerful queens, and also other kings,” said Guton. “Any one of these characters could have ended up being the star. But quite quickly we found this female lion and her cub we called Kio.”Finding the main character for the series was a relief. It could also have been a nightmare, given that 50% of lion cubs don’t make it to adulthood. Through parts of the rainy season, Kio couldn’t be followed by the crew as the plains in the Maasai Mara became impassable. At other times, Kio and his brothers were hardly seen for weeks. Every check-in with the field team started with a question: “How’s Kio — is he alive?”“You really have to surrender yourself to what fate had in store,” said Favreau. “We didn’t have any recourse to change the outcomes. I’m used to writing and creating shots and creating moments. Not knowing whether the lead character that emerged was going to survive through each rainy season was harrowing.”As the series exec producer, Favreau helped take approximately 1,000 hours of footage and turn it into a comprehensive, four-hour story. Like Disney’s “The Lion King,” Nat Geo’s “Lion” also tells the coming-of-age story of a male lion, which, Favreau said, was a fluke.“Less than half lion cubs survive to adulthood, so we didn’t know what was going to present itself,” said Favreau. “What ended up emerging was the story of this one young, small lion that kept surviving and prevailing and growing and emerging and eventually reaching adulthood and becoming a leader in his own right. So, it did echo a hero’s journey type story and ended up echoing a lot of Disney heroes and felt like it connected very much with ‘The Lion King.’ The fact that things played out the way that they did was not something we could have anticipated.”Although the story is reminiscent of “The Lion King” and Hans Zimmer composed the score for “Lion,” the series is real-life drama.“It’s not jaws and claws nor is it saccharine,” said Gunton. “It’s true. It’s what happens in nature. It’s sometimes tough. It’s sometimes beautiful. It’s sometimes heartwarming. It’s sometimes shocking. But nobody’s going to say, ‘Oh, that’s been Disneyfied,’ And nobody’s going to say, “Oh, that’s a bit tough. That’s a bit horrible. That’s a bit bloody.’ I think we’ve got the line pretty right.”“Lion” premieres on Aug. 19 on National Geographic and streams on Disney+ and Hulu on Aug. 20.“Lion” is produced by BBC Studios Natural History Unit for National Geographic. Favreau and Mike Gunton executive produce the series. Jane Atkins is series producer, and Simon Blakeney is co-executive producer. For National Geographic, Janet Han Vissering and Tom McDonald executive produce.

schema.headline: Jon Favreau on His First Documentary, National Geographic’s ‘Lion’: Not Knowing Whether the Lead Character Would Survive Was ‘Harrowing’

title: Amanda Waller Series, Wonder Woman Prequel ‘Paradise Lost’ No Longer in Active Development at DC Studios
description:
Two previously announced TV projects are being put on hold at DC Studios. 

	Variety has confirmed that both the Amanda Waller standalone series wit
body:
Two previously announced TV projects are being put on hold at DC Studios. 

	Variety has confirmed that both the Amanda Waller standalone series with Viola Davis and “Paradise Lost,” which would serve as a prequel to “Wonder Woman,” are no longer in active development. 

	Reps for DC Studios declined to comment. 


	“Waller” was first reported to be in the works in May 2022, roughly five months before James Gunn and Peter Safran were named the heads of what became known as DC Studios. “Paradise Lost,” meanwhile, was unveiled as part of Gunn and Safran’s initial slate of DC projects in January 2023. 
	

	Waller would have seen Davis return as the character she played in both David Ayer and Gunn’s “Suicide Squad” films. “Paradise Lost” would have taken place on the island of Themyscira before the birth of Wonder Woman. It should be noted that neither project was ever ordered to series. 


	Similarly, the “Booster Gold” show that Gunn and Safran announced as being in development in 2023 is also not moving forward, as noted by series writer David Jenkins. 

	Since taking over DC, Gunn and Safran have greenlit the upcoming HBO Green Lantern series “Lanterns” starring Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre and also oversaw the launch of “The Penguin,” though the latter show was picked up prior to their entry atop the DC Universe. They also launched the animated series “Creature Commandos,” which is returning for a second season. 

	DC Studios is also currently at work on a series in which Skyler Gisondo will reprise his “Superman” role as Jimmy Olson in a true crime mockumentary, with the first season set to focus on Gorilla Grodd. Jimmy Tatro will play Gorilla Grodd, with Tony Yacenda and Dan Perrault showrunning. 
	

	The Ankler first reported that “Waller” and “Paradise Lost” were not moving forward.

schema.headline: Amanda Waller Series, Wonder Woman Prequel ‘Paradise Lost’ No Longer in Active Development at DC Studios

title: Paramount Has Considered Creating Oversight Body for CNN in Warner Deal
description:
Every day, governments, newsmakers and politicians scrutinize the news reporting of CNN. Paramount Skydance wants to add to the list.

	The media co
body:
Every day, governments, newsmakers and politicians scrutinize the news reporting of CNN. Paramount Skydance wants to add to the list.

	The media conglomerate, whose efforts to acquire CNN parent Warner Bros. Discovery have stalled in federal court after a group of 12 attorneys general levied antitrust concerns against the proposed deal, has considered setting up an oversight committee to govern the news giant.


	“We always remain open to internal improvements to journalistic integrity,” Paramount  said in a statement. The Wall Street Journal previously reported the discussions, but executives at Warner Bros. Discovery considered a similar maneuver when they were working to split Warner’s streaming-and-studio assets from its cable properties last year, before Paramount made a bid for the company.
	

	The belief seems to be that an oversight board would help create the impression that Paramount takes CNN’s journalistic independence seriously, after its installation of entrepreneur and opinion journalist Bari Weiss has created drama and fostered skepticism about the state of CBS News. Weiss’ maneuvers at CBS, in particular her decision to oust top producers and correspondents from the long-running newsmagazine “60 Minutes,” has created controversy and spectacle for which few at the media conglomerate seemed prepared.

	Paramount CEO David Ellison has made governance of CNN a central issue in the debate over the Warner pact.  “The issue is whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN,” Ellison said in an opinion piece written last week for The New York Times. CNN has long been viewed antagonistically by the Trump administration, with President Trump lambasting its journalists many times during his first and second term, including well-known CNN faces like Kaitlan Collins. 
	

	There are growing fears within CNN that the Paramount acquisition would put the news outlet under Weiss’ aegis, leaving it open to programming and talent changes that are seen as being made to placate the current administration in power, rather than holding it to account. Inside CNN,  there is a strong concern that Paramount’s executives “don’t know or don’t care” about managing the news giant for profit or for the future, according to one staffer. 

	An oversight board could hinder Paramount in what are certain to be future efforts to wring synergies out of a combined company. Merging CBS News and CNN could reduce production and newsgathering costs. And yet, CBS News employs many workers represented by a union, while CNN does not. That dynamic has thwarted previous efforts over the years to combine the two news organizations. An oversight board aimed at ensuring an independent CNN might have a similar effect.

	An oversight entity could also not be worth the effort. Rupert Murdoch created a similar structure when he purchased The Wall Street Journal from its longtime owners, the Bancroft family, in 2007 for $5 billion. But there is little mention of such an entity today when the giant news outlet grapples with legal or operational matters. An oversight committee staffed by journalism experts, academics and executives that holds regular meetings with senior operators might have some bite. A group led by a motley group of friends and acquaintances that rarely engages with operating officers might be seen as toothless.

schema.headline: Paramount Has Considered Creating Oversight Body for CNN in Warner Deal

title: EA’s New ‘Star Wars’ Game Was Inspired by an AMC Revolutionary War TV Series and a Love for Turn-Based Tactics
description: Electronic Arts’ “Star Wars Zero Company” will be the latest in a long, long line of video games set in Lucasfilm’s galaxy far, far away. But this u
body:
Electronic Arts’ “Star Wars Zero Company” will be the latest in a long, long line of video games set in Lucasfilm’s galaxy far, far away. But this upcoming single-player turn-based tactics title developed by Bit Reactor aims to be different from all the Star Wars games that have come before — and not just because it’s the franchise’s first turn-based tactics game. 

	“It would be very easy for us to want to come at Orion [Kellogg, Lucasfilm Games executive producer] and say, ‘Orion, I want to make a game with Yoda and Anakin and whatever,’ right? But people can’t attach to those characters because they already have an opinion of those characters,” Greg Foertsch, head of “Star Wars Zero Company” developer Bit Reactor, tells Variety. “From the very onset of this and looking at some other things that I’ve done, I wanted to make this where you had characters that you could latch onto that you could imprint on, and that you could feel connected to.” 
	

	Set to launch Aug. 27 for PC, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S, “Star Wars Zero Company” puts players into the role of former Galactic Republic officer Hawks, who they’re able to fully customize (including their choice of a masculine or feminine voice, performed by Jonathan Freeman and Erica Luttrell, respectively). Hawks leads Zero Company, an unconventional outfit of professionals for hire from across the galaxy, which includes a Clone Trooper, a Mandalorian, a Jedi Padawan and more. Throughout the game, players must hunt down and stop Kundri Fathom (Rekha Sharma), the ruthless leader of the Separatist-aligned cult known as the Infinite Coil.
	

	“Hawks is a very authentic role, but there is no canon identity for Hawks,” Lucasfilm Games executive producer Orion Kellogg says. “It gets to be you, and you get to impress yourself upon that character. But also the events that happen, they really happened in Star Wars. They really have impact, and they really have a place. So it’s a little bit of the best of all worlds.”

	Foertsch says a major inspiration for the game’s narrative approach was the AMC drama series “Turn.” That show, which debuted in 2014 and had a four-season run, followed both notable and nameless figures during the Revolutionary War.

	“Much like that show ‘Turn,’ where it’s surrounded by the Revolutionary War, there’s this thing happening inside of it, and you’ve got Cornwallis, and you’ve got Benedict Arnold, and you’ve got Washington, and they all pepper you from outside this orbit,” Foertsch says. “So you’re familiar with this stuff. You’ve heard all those names. You know what’s happening in the Revolutionary War. But then there’s the story happening with these characters that I’ve grown accustomed to, care about, and their relationships. And so that’s probably the biggest similarity to our approach to this. But we wanted to make sure that those characters were characters that you felt like you had a connection to, and that spoke to you in a way that didn’t bring so much backstory that you couldn’t craft your own theories about your version of Hawks, for example.”

	From the Lucasfilm Games side, Kellogg says the priority was “a story that felt ownable and something that felt authentic,” which meant using well-known characters like Anakin Skywalker (voiced by “Star Wars: Clone Wars” alum Matt Lanter, who is reprising his role from that series) but sparingly and on the periphery of the story.

	“We come back to the word ‘authentic’ a lot, but you’re not going to tell an authentic story about the time the All Stars got together and beat up on the other All Stars,” Kellogg says. “There’s great games where you can do that, but this game I think benefited from zooming in and from making everybody that you’re going on this adventure with feel real, and as we do that, we just find natural opportunities.”

	Kellogg adds: “We didn’t start with, how do we get this character involved or that character involved as we go. We go, who would make sense there, and our Lucasfilm Rolodex starts to open up, and character availability starts to get hooked, and that’s the best way to do it.”
	

	The Clone Wars era was selected not just because it’s a fan-favorite chapter in the Star Wars saga, but because “it had the most answers to the questions that we needed answered,” Foertsch says. “It allows us to tell a story that is unique, but still surrounded by really familiar elements that, if you’re a fan, you’re going to appreciate, if you’re not a fan, you’re going to come along for the ride,” he continued. “But it gave us a lot of freedom, frankly, to introduce the things we wanted to introduce mechanically, that also marry up super well with what’s going on in the canon.”

	As for the choice to make a turn-based tactics game in the vein of “XCOM” (a franchise near and dear to Firaxis Games vet Foertsch and his studio Bit Reactor as a whole), a genre that’s not the most accessible to the average, everyday gamer, the “Zero Company” dev says “there’s a lot of things you can do to remove some of the barriers from a user experience perspective that we focus pretty heavily on.”

	“I think the narrative, frankly, can really help deliver the payload for how to play the game and what matters,” Foertsch says. “And if you don’t see it as this separate thing that you tack on later, if you approach the story like we did with this, where it’s woven into the mechanics of the game, it’s woven into the original concepts of what we’re doing. We say it’s about starting with Star Wars, we’re not kidding, we really do start there. I think that really can help Star Wars fans understand the mechanics and work themselves into this. It’s like you’re trying a different kind of music, but you still understand this music. You still get it. You can like it. You can go follow the beat. We can drive you through it. But if you’re a tactics fan, it’s got all the depth and mechanics and challenge that you might want. They’re not mutually exclusive. It’s making it accessible, not making it simple. I think that’s always been a driving concern for us from the very, very beginning.”

	Kellogg says the tactics genre really appealed to Lucasfilm when planning for “Star Wars Zero Company” as its latest game because “Star Wars does not shy away from choice with consequence.”

	“That gives texture to any good narrative or any good experience, so we welcome that,” Kellogg says. “But we want you to be wowed by what you’re seeing — the size and scale of the Clone Wars, the beautiful art that the team has put together, the incredible music is going to pull you into the experience. So all of this stuff, it’s going to lessen the barriers. And on the Star Wars side as well, we say no homework required. That’s sort of a mantra for us. We want to make sure we tell you the story from the beginning. All of that said, there’s going to be challenge where you’d expect there to be, and of course, if you feel like you need to loosen something up, we have options, we have settings, we have all of that stuff. But we do encourage you to embrace the full experience.”

schema.headline: EA’s New ‘Star Wars’ Game Was Inspired by an AMC Revolutionary War TV Series and a Love for Turn-Based Tactics

title: Salli Richardson-Whitfield on Making Emmy History With ‘Task’ and ‘The Gilded Age’
description: An hour into Salli Richardson-Whitfield’s directorial debut, she was left to sink or swim.This was 2011, and Richardson-Whitefield was standing behi
body:
An hour into Salli Richardson-Whitfield’s directorial debut, she was left to sink or swim.This was 2011, and Richardson-Whitefield was standing behind the camera on the set of Syfy’s quirky small-town comedy “Eureka” talking to series creator Matt Hastings. She had been asking to try her hand at directing and finally got the shot in Season 4.
	“I remember it was the first day. I was about an hour in, and he just looked at me and he goes, ‘You got it,’ and he left,” she tells Variety. “But by the end of that first episode, I remember going, “Oh, I got this.’ Was my first episode of TV my best work? Probably not, but I understood the assignment and I loved it.”Fifteen years later, she’s still got this, and she’s in the history books to prove it. At last year’s Primetime Emmys, Richardson-Whitfield became the first Black woman ever nominated for directing a drama series. This year, she one-upped herself and became the first woman to have two nominations in that category at the same time. At next month’s ceremony, her name will be called for both the penultimate episode of the gritty freshman crime drama “Task,” and the luminous Season 3 finale of “The Gilded Age” — both HBO series on which she serves as an executive producer.“I actually wish I didn’t have to talk about it because I shouldn’t be the first at this point,” she says of the benchmarks. But for that reason, she feels a responsibility to make sure that every time she’s behind the camera, she’s at her best.“It’s why I go into these places and these spaces, and I work so hard,” she adds. “If I do a bad job, I don’t want any woman, I don’t want any Black woman, to come behind me and be judged by my failure. If you go on a set, maybe 90% of the directors will be men. So if one of them is bad, it doesn’t matter. They’re not judged as a whole group. But if you’ve never had a woman, or you’ve never had a Black woman, work with you before, if I fail, then it becomes [symptomatic of us all]. So, I really take it seriously, and I think this is my purpose and my calling.”She felt that weight on “Task,” which was the new kid on the Sunday-night-primetime-HBO block and a critical hit last fall. But more importantly, it stoked the kind of fire in Richardson-Whitfield that she craves in her directing projects.“Every new kind of genre that I’m able to attack, for me, is a challenge,” she says. “Can I conquer it? Can I be the best at this? The particular episode that’s nominated was that challenge for me.”The episode in question is the turning point of the series. After tragic losses and setbacks, FBI agent Tom Brandis (Mark Ruffalo) is finally converging on his target: working-class family man Robbie Prendergrast (Tom Pelphrey), who has been robbing trap houses belonging to a biker gang and stripping them of their drug money. Built around an on-foot pursuit in the woods, the episode is a masterclass in tension building and sacrificial storytelling, claiming more than one of the main characters by the end of the hour.In other words, it was a pivotal episode that had to land the gut punch this series wanted to communicate. “I remember [exec vice president and head of drama] Francesca Orsi at HBO saying, ‘This better be the best wooded scene and 20 minutes of a fight scene I’ve ever seen in my life,’” Richardson-Whitfield says with a laugh.Again, challenge accepted. The episode is a directing feat she says was made infinitely more satisfying by “Task” creator Brad Inglesby’s writing across the series. “He just writes these really interesting, flawed people — good and bad,” she says. “And then the opportunity to do such huge sequences of action mixed with great drama, it’s exactly what I want as a director.”But as an executive producer, she’s also been able to help craft everything around the episodes she helms. For instance, all of the Season 1 episodes were directed by two people — either her or Jeremiah Zagar. In Season 2, she will return to direct, this time alongside an all-female directing lineup. Helping fine-tune the vision and the look of the series, even when she isn’t the credited director, has become a key component of what excites Richard-Whitfield.“Sometimes, we’re shooting the whole season at the same time, it’s like making two feature films at once,” she says. “It’s just becoming something that I do now, and I enjoy it and it feels like a comfortable space. Coming in and just doing one episode would feel very odd to me now.”Fortunately, she’s in it for the long haul with both “Task” and “The Gilded Age.” On the latter, she cut her teeth not just as a director with the support of creator Julian Fellowes, but also as a multi-hyphenate creative force on set. She covets working through her vision for a scene with writers and crew, even breaking out massive storyboards to walk through it. She did that with the climax of “The Gilded Age” finale, which weaves together the soapy happenings of two simultaneous high-society balls. She intercut scenes from one with the other, creating a seamless but stylish bridge between two social circles and two racial classes.“I have these beautiful homes, this beautiful wardrobe and these amazing actors, and when I think about that sequence and every entrance into the ball, I wanted to make a meal out of it visually,” she says. “All of it was very planned. What are our connected pieces? What is the camera movement that’s going to lead us in and out of each ball? What is the dress swirl that’ll swirl us into the other ball? I had storyboards. Everyone teases me about my storyboards. But I’m all over the wall when we’re shooting.”It’s her process — one she has refined but also embraced as she’s come to understand that sense of purpose she found in this history-making stage of her career. She trusts her gut, even when not everyone sees the vision right away. During one of the balls, Peggy (Denée Benton) gets her fairy-tale moment when William Kirkland (Jordan Donica) defies his prejudiced mother (Phylicia Rashad) and cuts through the dance floor to propose to her in front of everyone.“At the time, people were like, ‘We don’t know about this slow-motion shot into Peggy’s proposal,’” she says. “I told them to just trust me. It’s Cinderella, it’s romantic, and I know it’s a little mushy, a little over the top, but it’s the thing that people come up and talk to me about the most.”She’s got this. Whether it is the grand ballrooms of the highest societies or the last-resort Hail Marys of small-town families clawing to survive, Richardson-Whitfield has earned her history-making nominations. But there’s always another hill to climb and category to conquer. So, might she tackle comedy next?“Maybe a dark dramedy,” she says with a laugh. “I don’t think I’m going to be doing my sitcom half-hour multicam anytime soon. But if I could get a ‘Hacks,’ then yes! I could do ‘Hacks’ all day.”

schema.headline: Salli Richardson-Whitfield on Making Emmy History With ‘Task’ and ‘The Gilded Age’

title: ‘Assassin’s Creed’ Creator’s New Action-Adventure Game ‘1666: Amsterdam’ Sets Early Access Release (Gaming News Roundup)
description:
Panache Digital Games announced “1666: Amsterdam” will release in Early Access on Aug. 25.

	From “Assassin’s Creed” series creator Patrice Désilets
body:
Panache Digital Games announced “1666: Amsterdam” will release in Early Access on Aug. 25.

	From “Assassin’s Creed” series creator Patrice Désilets, the dark, third-person narrative action-adventure game unravels a mystery across Amsterdam. Players take on the role of Noa, the Collector, who wields witchcraft to uncover “Originals,” demonic entities hiding behind human faces.


	The Early Access version of “1666: Amsterdam” will be available for PC via Steam and Epic Games Store for $29.99 on Aug. 25. The EA edition “will include the first piece of the campaign, expected to take approximately 15 hours to playthrough.” 
	

	Per the description for the game, “A cycle is ending. Another one is beginning. Take part in Noa’s Commencement as she inherits the mantle of the Collector. Unravel a mystery that spans centuries. Choose the companion that will walk beside you. Follow the traces left behind in a city shaped by secrets, power, and memory. This is where everything begins.”


	Watch a new gameplay feature for “1666: Amsterdam” below. The video gives an in-depth look at the game’s mechanics, combat and the day and night cycle. It also showcases the unique playing styles of lead characters Noa and Aaron as they hunt Originals across Amsterdam.



	See more gaming news from this week in the roundup below.
	
		AWARDS	

	The 2027 BAFTA Games Awards are now open for entries, albeit with a few key changes.

	BAFTA will now open the Evolving Game category to a member-wide vote across all rounds, while the organization has reaffirmed its commitment to “outstanding human achievement” in the face of concerns around AI. Entry fees have also been revised, with a new 25% discount for eligible independent and small developers.
	

	“With this year’s updates to eligibility and voting, the Awards continue to celebrate outstanding human creativity, craft and innovation, while evolving to reflect the way the sector is changing,” BAFTA’s director of awards Kelly Smith said in a statement. “I’m looking forward to seeing the exceptional work that will be recognized in 2027.”

	Entries will close on Friday, Sept. 18 for games released between November 15, 2025 and July 31, 2026, while entries will close on Friday, November 6 for games released between Aug. 1 and November 19, 2026.
	
		MONETIZATION	

	Mobile game developer and publisher Scopely announced a content creator initiative for “Monopoly Go!”

	The Go! Friends Creator Fund allows content creators to develop original ideas that adapt the themes of “Monopoly Go!’”s gameplay into their storytelling formats. 

	“At its core, Monopoly Go! is designed to give friends new reasons to connect, compete and have fun together. That same idea is the creative starting point for the GO! Friends Creator Fund,” said Jamie Berger, senior vice president of marketing for Monopoly Go! at Scopely. “We believe in providing creators with freedom to explore the themes of friendship in their own voice and format, while staying true to what works for their audience. Our goal is to move beyond one-off, transactional partnerships and build original entertainment alongside creators, and we’re excited to welcome more of them into the Monopoly Go! universe.”

	The fund supports creators’ artistic direction for their audiences, rather than relying on predetermined campaigns.
	
		EXEC SHUFFLE	

	Sandbox Group has appointed senior brand and entertainment marketing executive Amanda Klecker as chief marketing officer. 

	Klecker will oversee marketing and brand strategy across the life skill platform’s digital portfolio. She previously served as the head of marketing and franchise at pocket.watch, as well as working in marketing leadership at ViacomCBS/Paramount and Martha Stewart. Throughout her career, she’s received accolades such as Chief Marketer Top Women in Marketing: Disruptors, Cynopsis Top Women in Marketing: Marketing Trailblazers and 40 Under 40: NYC TV Week. 

	The platform’s global digital portfolio has 50 million monthly users, 1 billion app downloads and 500 million monthly page views. Its flagship brands include PlayKids Learning, Coolmath Games and Focus. 
	
	
		RELEASE DATES	

	“Ghost of Yōtei Complete Edition” releases Oct. 1, featuring a narrative expansion, new single player combat survival mode and additional updates.

	“Ghost of Yōtei: Echoes of Sekigahara” is a new narrative expansion for “Ghost of Yōtei.” Split between present day and flashbacks to Atsu’s time on the mainland, players explore a previously unseen valley.

	“Ghost of Yōtei: Most Wanted” is a new single-player combat survival mode. Players use their unique combat specialty to take down enemies, earn perks and unlock additional playable characters.

	The full edition will be available for purchase for PS5. It includes the main “Ghost of Yōtei” game, “Ghost of Yōtei Legends” online co-op mode, “Echoes of Sekigahara,” “Most Wanted,” the in-game content included in the Digital Deluxe Edition and the Charm of Hokkyokusei.
	
		TRAILERS	

	Dropout released the trailer for the new season of its hit tabletop, role-playing game actual play show “Dimension 20.”

	“Dimension 20: Toylight” features the players, known as the Intrepid Heroes, as a band of toys rising up to defend the enchanted Toylight, the last flicker of a dying child’s imagination.

	“Toylight” is led by Game Master Brennan Lee Mulligan and stars Emily Axford, Ally Beardsley, Brian Murphy, Zac Oyama, Siobhan Thompson and Lou Wilson.

	The season premieres Sept. 16 on Dropout, with six episodes that debut weekly on Wednesdays.

body:
Hayley Williams’ band Power Snatch has released their second project “EP2,” which they surprise-dropped on Bandcamp.

	“EP2” features four songs including “Machete,” “New Legs,” “Born Dead” and “Hell Is a Highway.” The group posted on Instagram to help announce the project, setting the song “Machete” against footage from the 1973 animated art film “Fantastic Planet.”

	Williams officially unveiled Power Snatch earlier this year while hosting a show on Apple Music alongside Power Snatch band member Daniel James, who served as a producer on her third solo album “Ego Death at a Bachelorette Party.” Power Snatch initially soft-launched the band with the release of their first single “DMs” on Bandcamp in December, followed by the debut of “Assignment” on Apple Music and “EP1” in February. This past June, Power Snatch followed with two more singles, “Great” and “Training,” with Tiberius b.
	

	Outside of Power Snatch, Williams has spent a good part of the year on her “Hayley Williams at a Bachelorette Party” tour in support of her 2025 album. The tour kicked off in Atlanta this past March and continued across the world before concluding in Dublin on June 30.

	Williams is currently gearing up for another tour, “The Hayley Williams Show,” which sees her upgrading to bigger venues. The trek kicks off on September 3 at West Palm Beach’s iTHINK Financial Amphitheatre, making its way through the United States before rounding out its run in Puerto Rico on November 28. Williams will also perform three subsequent dates in Mexico in January.

title: ‘The Matrix’ Director Lilly Wachowski Says Hollywood Won’t Finance Her $10 Million Thriller Because It’s Got a ‘Wall-to-Wall Trans Cast’
description: Filmmaker Lilly Wachowski is working to get her next project, “The Hunted,” out of late-stage production. But the “Bound” and “Matrix” director says
body:
Filmmaker Lilly Wachowski is working to get her next project, “The Hunted,” out of late-stage production. But the “Bound” and “Matrix” director says nobody in Hollywood wants to finance the thriller, which is budgeted at around $10 million, because of its trans representation.

	“People like it, but they really don’t want to make it because it’s [got a] wall-to-wall trans cast,” Wachowski said on KCRW’s “The Business” podcast last Friday. “I have to get creative and figure out different ways that I can get this in front of people.”
	

	“This is a script that was extremely important for me to write,” she continued. “It was a response to what is happening in the world for trans people, and it gave me a hugely cathartic receptacle to dump all of my anger and rage and frustration into.”


	Wachowski co-wrote the project with her partner, Mickey Ray Mahoney. While facing difficulties getting “The Hunted” off the ground, which is currently in development through Anarchists United and Natasha Lyonne’s Ariadne banner, Wachowski assembled a live table read at Los Angeles’ Dynasty Typewriter theater from Aug. 7-8.

	“I’m just going to go out and I’m going to grab that trans joy with all of my friends,” Wachowski said of her thought process. “It’s not the thing that I had imagined it was going to be, but the end result is the same.”

	Wachowski is known for her many sci-fi collaborations with her sister, Lana Wachowski. After directing 1999’s “The Matrix,” the two went on to helm sequels like “The Matrix Reloaded” and “The Matrix Revolutions.” The pair also directed the cult classic “Speed Racer,” “Cloud Atlas” and “Jupiter Ascending.”

title: The ‘Paranormal Activity’ Stage Show Has Audiences Screaming and Laughing. Can It Be Broadway’s Surprise New Hit?
description: Broadway producers traditionally gauge audience reaction by warm applause at the end of Act 1 or a standing ovation during curtain call. But “Parano
body:
Broadway producers traditionally gauge audience reaction by warm applause at the end of Act 1 or a standing ovation during curtain call. But “Paranormal Activity” producer Simon Friend laughs while recalling the profane reaction of a man scared for his life while watching the play: “Fuck! Fuck! Fuck! Fuck!”

	“Paranormal Activity,” which opens at the August Wilson Theatre on Aug. 14, was inspired by the 2007 thriller that made $194 million at the box office on a budget of $15,000. The story centers on James and Lou, a young couple who encounter increasingly disturbing happenings in their new home.
	

	Make no mistake: “Paranormal Activity” is intended to be a horror movie onstage — and designed to draw a much different audience than the Great White Way is used to entertaining. 


	“I hope people who might not go to see plays but know the movie take a chance, that the thought of being terrified in New York City is a thrill,” says director Felix Barrett. “Hopefully get a taste for how potent and powerful live theatricality can be.” The production premiered in Leeds, England, before transferring to the West End and then playing in markets like Los Angeles, D.C. and Chicago.

	Friend sees opportunity in the cultural moment, with indie upstarts like “Backrooms” and “Obsession” recently topping the box office. But Broadway is a different beast, and the real question is whether horror audiences are willing to go beyond their local multiplex in search of frights. Success on the stage hasn’t come easily: “Grey House,” from “Paranormal Activity” writer Levi Holloway, closed after three months, and slashers-turned-musicals “Evil Dead: The Musical” and “American Psycho” didn’t last long in New York City.
	

	“It costs $15 compared to what a Broadway ticket costs,” Friend says. “They’re different things, and it does mean just by virtue of the cost of it — which is obviously related to the cost of doing it — it’s going for a slightly different market. But a movie like ‘Obsession’ is a really simple story that’s brilliantly told and wonderfully entertaining, which I hope is what we’ve got with ‘Paranormal Activity.’ That can actually reach outside of those who would consider themselves the horror audience.”

	Friend initially optioned the rights from Paramount Pictures, which had eventually turned the film into a seven-chapter series, with an eighth installment on the way next year. Onstage horror has a storied history in his native England, where some of Alfred Hitchcock’s most acclaimed work was based on stage adaptations, such as “Dial M for Murder” and “Rope,” and the supernatural show “The Woman in Black” ran from 1989 to 2023.He found collaborators with Barrett, who co-created the popular, free-roaming take on “Macbeth” called “Sleep No More,” which ran for 14 years in New York City, and Holloway, whose “Grey House” ran on Broadway in 2023 and starred Laurie Metcalf and Tatiana Maslany.Early in the development phase, the trio sought the help of illusion designer Chris Fisher, a magic expert who helped bring the showstopping effects to life in “Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.” Together, they hoped to create a show which would shock and scare audiences.Instead of bringing in Fisher at the end, his work was an integral part of the scriptwriting. Levi focused the story on James and Lou, newlyweds who move from Chicago to England at the top of the play. He’s a skeptic, she’s a believer, but once things start going bump in the night, tension quickly escalates. Fisher was in charge of creating said bumps.“There was a skeletal script that Levi had done,” Fisher says. “Myself, Felix and Levi sat around a table, and there were a couple of moments that Levi had written in, but then we started coming around. I always say to a writer, ‘Don’t write what you think can be done, just write what you want to do.’ Then it’s my job to try and put that onto stage. And so we just threw crazy ideas in and Levi very carefully laced those through.”

	Through clever lighting, sound and visual trickery, the production forces the audience to stay alert for glimpses of ghosts or demonic happenings. The ambitious staging literally rips the fourth wall off a two-story house, giving a voyeuristic view into the kitchen, living room, bathroom and bedroom. Much of the two-hour run time is spent with eyes darting to darkened corners, checking for rogue shadows or apparitions whenever a ripple of recognition runs through another part of the audience.

	In fact, the biggest difference between “Paranormal Activity” and other stage productions may be the vocal crowd, gasping or clapping at the more intricate scares. During a recent performance in Boston, there were two big moments of comic relief: At one point Travis A. Knight, who plays James, casually popped his shirt off, causing an audience member to moan loudly; later, a knock at the front door inspired someone in the orchestra section to yell, “It’s ICE!”

	“We weren’t expecting it,” Barrett says. “First we thought, ‘This is a theater, and in a theater, you don’t heckle and you don’t cackle. You don’t go, “Don’t go up the stairs!”’ It’s just not the etiquette. But from preview one of this, we’re like, ‘Oh my gosh, the audience is treating this as though it’s a movie.’ The behavior is completely different. So we just lean into it and celebrate it.”

	The creative team also has a big vote of confidence in horror mogul Jason Blum, who produced the original film and signed on as a producer of the play. Despite being based on a film that he says “changed the trajectory of my life,” he went to a Los Angeles performance bracing for disappointment. 
	

	“I honestly had very low expectations, not because of who was involved, not because it was ‘Paranormal Activity,’ but over many years I’ve seen many attempts at people trying to do a live stage event and make it actually scary or unnerving,” Blum says. “For a multitude of reasons, it’s just much easier to do on film. For sound and special effects reasons and the way you can force people’s eye anywhere you want by the shots that you choose in movies, you cannot do that with live stage. You can’t force people to look. The only way for a good scare is to be looking at something and then the scare comes somewhere else, and it’s very hard to do with stage. Everyone always invites me to anything that’s scary, and I’m always interested in going to see it. I love theater, I see a lot of theater, I’m on the board of The Public Theater. I’m always intrigued, and it almost never happens that it’s scary. This was actually a really satisfying, scary experience, so I decided we wanted to be more involved.” 

	If the team can pull off a Broadway hit with “Paranormal Activity,” they have other big ideas for horrifying audiences onstage. 

	“Absolutely there are other titles that we would love to do,” Barrett says. “This feels like the start of a new sub-genre of theatre where an audience can call and response and be part of it. They can be cathartically vocal in their appreciation of the horror of it all.” 

	Fisher says that sharing his childlike sense of wonder — about both magic and the theater — with audiences is the most wonderful part of the production. 

	“I started in magic when I was four, and I’ve worked in theater all my life,” he says. “To bring the two together in the last 15 years has been the best experience because I’m that younger kid all the time. I really enjoy seeing people of all ages feeling that now as well, coming out of theater and feeling energized and pumped from what they’ve seen, and they want to see more theater because of it as well.”

            Get ready for a new White House Press Secretary ... President Trump says Karoline Leavitt is stepping down from the job.
      
    
            Trump announced Karoline's upcoming career move in a Truth Social post Wednesday ... saying she's leaving the gig at the end of the month so she can spend more time with her kids and family.
      
    
            Karoline gave birth in May to a daughter ... her second child.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Trump says Karoline will be one of his top outside advisors and continue to be an influential voice within the GOP.
      

            It sounds like this is Karoline's choice ... Trump says he totally understands and respects her decision and praises her as one of the best White House Press Secretaries in American history.
      
    
            Karoline started her current role in January 2025, at the beginning of Trump's second term.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            No word who is on the short list to replace Karoline.
      
    
            Trump had 4 press secretaries in his first term ... and now he will have at least two in his second term.
      
    
            It will be interesting to see who lands the job.

title: Tyga's $TARFACE Album Gets Rare 0/10 Pitchfork Rating For Using A.I.
description:
Tyga
                          Album Gets Rare Pitchfork Goose Egg For Using A.I.
body:
Tyga
                          Album Gets Rare Pitchfork Goose Egg For Using A.I.
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 12, 2026
                            11:40 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Tyga's having a rough rollout for his latest album ... because Pitchfork just gave it an impressively awful 0/10 rating ... and it sounds like robots did him no favors.
      
    
            Reviewer Drew Miller deemed the record "slop pop," calling it "smug and complacent and depressing."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            He continued by delivering a lethal blow ... "Its very existence has made the world a worse place."
      
    
            Miller slammed the musician for admittingly using A.I. on the project, saying ... "I'm not saying the record is A.I.-generated; all I'm saying is that I was personally able to generate a song that sounded exactly like '$TARFACE,' assuming it had included a song about a critic trying to write a review of a Tyga album."
      

            In Vibe interview from earlier this month, Tyga copped to using A.I. as a tool, saying ... "And I know people are going to be mad about me saying this, but it's where technology is going. It's no different than when Auto-Tune came out."
      
    
            This was a bit of a pivot from his People interview published a week before the Vibe piece, where he claimed ... "Everything that we used was stuff that they used in the '80s."
      
    
            He continued ... "Now everybody uses the plug-ins and everything in Pro Tools. But we used a lot of the original hardware, and it just really gave it that warm sound."
      
    
            Miller goes in on the artist, dissecting Tyga's lack of "human breath" and similarities to Fenix Flexin's song "Rubberz," which people speculate was also made using A.I. elements.
      
    
            He called out the music industry as a whole for encouraging A.I.-generated music to get out of paying songwriters and session musicians for their time and art.
      
    
            According to Miller, the result in Tyga's case is an album he says is "smug and complacent, an amalgam of '80s synth-pop and disco slapped together by someone who's seemingly never cared to listen to one synth-pop or disco record in his life."
      
    
            But hey, at least Tyga can say he accomplished something only a select few artists have ever done ... scoring a zilch from Pitchfork.

title: Luigi Mangione's Team Negotiating Plea Deal with Feds, State Case in Jeopardy
description:
Luigi Mangione
                          Serious Plea Bargain Negotiations Underway with Feds
body:
Luigi Mangione
                          Serious Plea Bargain Negotiations Underway with Feds
                          Could Upend State Case
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 12, 2026
                            11:17 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 12, 2026
                                1:00 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            MAJOR twist in the Luigi Mangione case ... his legal team is in serious negotiations with federal prosecutors, sources tell TMZ, and it could have a dramatic impact on his fate.
      
    
            Sources with direct knowledge tell TMZ ... the negotiations are "real," and it involves a possible guilty plea to murder, but the twist comes with sentencing. We're told one of the "possibilities" is an open plea where sentencing is not negotiated, but left to the judge after an extensive hearing. That would allow the defense to present mitigating factors -- including Luigi's strong feels about health care and corporate greed that altered his mental state -- that could lead to a sentence more favorable than life in prison.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The implications here are dramatic. When someone is charged in both federal and state court for the same offense and the federal case resolves first, the state cannot prosecute based on double jeopardy. Paul Manafort successfully made this argument in a New York state court when he was prosecuted for fraud back in 2019.
      

            What's more, even if -- for some reason -- the double jeopardy argument would not fly, then Luigi's lawyers could use the defense of extreme emotional disturbance without fear it would come back to haunt him in the federal case. That would effectively allow Luigi to put the health care system on trial if the state case goes forward.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Mind you, based on the current state of New York law, it would seem the state case against Luigi would disappear based on double jeopardy, if a federal plea bargain is reached.
      
    
            Stay tuned!

title: Kansas Father Kills Wife, Four Kids in Murder-Suicide
description:
Kansas Murder-Suicide
                          Father Kills Wife, 4 Kids Then Calls 911
body:
Kansas Murder-Suicide
                          Father Kills Wife, 4 Kids Then Calls 911
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 12, 2026
                            11:56 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            A Kansas father shot and killed his wife and four young children before dying by suicide ... according to law enforcement.
      
    
            Winfield Police Chief Robbie DeLong says a 911 call came in Tuesday morning from a man claiming he'd killed his entire family and was getting ready to kill himself.
      
    
            Officers heard a gunshot when they arrived at the house and set up a perimeter before entering the home ... discovering six people dead inside.
      
    
            Authorities identified the suspect as Ronald H. Williams Sr., who died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
      
    
            His wife, Kelly L. George, and his 4 children -- Carol Williams, Ronald Williams Jr., Sarah Williams and Kelly Magee-Williams -- were all found dead in the home.
      
    
            All of the kids were under the age of 10.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            DeLong said they'd gotten calls claiming Ronald Sr. was acting "erratic" and "aggressive" over the past few weeks, allegedly confronting and yelling at people.
      
    
            But the chief said that, at the time, the alleged incidents were "not enough really to act on," saying "nothing indicated we'd be where we are."
      
    
            Multiple outlets report that Ronald Sr. was a registered sex offender -- he'd been convicted back in 1998 of attempted indecent liberties with a child after an alleged incident involving a 15-year-old girl.
      
    
            Kelly George was 44, Carol was 9, Ronald Jr. was 7, Sarah was 5, and Kelly Magee-Williams was 3.
      
    
            RIP
